title: Who could be behind hoax bomb threats to European air travel?
description: The warnings came in thick and fast, targeting one airline or airport after another. In nearly all cases - London's Heathrow airport being a notable e
body: The warnings came in thick and fast, targeting one airline or airport after another. In nearly all cases - London's Heathrow airport being a notable exception - they were taken to be credible enough to divert the aircraft in question, or even in Italy's case, to scramble fighter jets to escort it. They all turned out to be false, which does not, of course, mean that the next ones will not  be real.It is hardly surprising that the simultaneous, co-ordinated nature of these airline hoaxes, coupled with other malicious actions across Europe, are causing some people to point the finger of suspicion at Russia. Following a series of cyber-attacks and mysterious drone sightings over sensitive sites earlier this year, in the past few days we have seen the remote hacking of supermarket freezers, as well as a blood bank, a suspicious incident on Poland's border with Russia, and in August a drone attack Germany's Leipzig Halle airport which its interior minister publicly blamed on Moscow.So is Russia behind this?There are many who argue, based purely on circumstantial evidence, that this must surely be yet another example of "hybrid", "grey zone" or "sub-threshold" warfare - actions that damage a nation's infrastructure or society but which tend to be anonymous, deniable and which fall short of triggering Nato's Article 5 and thereby mobilising a response by the West.Moscow is certainly furious with Nato for supporting Ukraine and, in doing so, frustrating the Kremlin's plans to swallow up that country and effectively terminate its independence. Russian bloggers have also suggested that, if Ukraine's drones are currently making Russia's airports unsafe, and Western sanctions are blocking Russian airlines from European airspace, then why shouldn't Western nations feel the same pain?But as of Thursday evening no hard evidence had emerged linking the airline hoaxes to Russia, Iran or any proxy groups controlled by them. There is the email threat sent on Thursday morning to airport authorities in Rome, purporting to be from "Fighters of the Male State". That name likely refers to the Russian group Muzhskoi Legion or "Male Legion", an ultra-right group with such extreme views it was banned by a Moscow court in 2021. Yet, it retained tens of thousands of online followers on Telegram as it cheered on the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in the following year.But the email sent to Rome, even if genuine - and who is to say it is not another group hiding behind that name? - is unlikely to provide the leads that police and airport authorities need to pin down who is generating these hoaxes and why.For national police forces, airport authorities and transport ministries trying to work out who is behind these hoaxes and how best to mitigate their effect when they happen again, the task is not to go with who they think might be the most likely culprits but instead to follow the cold, hard leads - if they can find them.

schema.headline: Who could be behind hoax bomb threats to European air travel?

title: The Pitt and ER are similar enough for lawsuit to proceed, judge rules
description: US drama The Pitt is similar enough to medical series ER for a lawsuit against its producers to progress, a court in the US has ruled. The widow of Mi
body: US drama The Pitt is similar enough to medical series ER for a lawsuit against its producers to progress, a court in the US has ruled. The widow of Michael Crichton, who created ER, argues The Pitt is effectively a reboot of the series, which has been made without proper permission or credit. Sherri Crichton says her husband's contract included a "frozen rights" provision that prohibited any spin-offs, sequels or reboots of ER being made without his express consent.A three-judge panel said there are "clear and numerous similarities between The Pitt and ER," which means the case can go ahead. Warner Bros previously described the lawsuit as "baseless" and sought to have it dismissed.Listing the similarities between the two shows, the court cited the emergency room setting, the fast pace, use of medical jargon, graphic depictions of injuries, and younger doctors fresh from medical school being trained. "We find the details here suffice for a prima facie case," the judges said.It means the case will now go to a jury trial in Los Angeles Superior Court.But the judges dismissed separate claims against actor-producer Noah Wyle, executive producer John Wells and showrunner R Scott Gemmill.The justices said there was insufficient evidence to show the three producers were aware they could be violating Crichton's contractual rights.ER launched in 1994, based on original screenplay written by Crichton. It starred George Clooney, Anthony Edwards, Eriq La Salle and Maria Bello, and aired 331 episodes over the next 15 years.The show, which followed a group of doctors working in an emergency room in Chicago, was a hit with viewers and critics, and won 23 Emmy Awards during its run including outstanding drama series.Discussions about a possible reboot of the show began in 2020, and studio Warner Bros spent months negotiating with Crichton's estate.Those talks were reported to have collapsed over credit and financial guarantees, and producers began developing The Pitt in its place.But Sherri Crichton and the John Michael Crichton Trust argue the show is a rebranded but uncredited reboot of ER, using the same formula, pacing, style and setting, rather than an entirely original series. They said producers "simply moved the show from Chicago to Pittsburgh, rebranded it The Pitt, and ploughed ahead without any attribution or compensation for Crichton and his heirs". Many actors and creatives from ER also work on The Pitt, including Wyle, Gemmill and Wells.After legal action began in 2024, Warner Bros Television said in a statement that the lawsuit was "baseless", arguing that The Pitt was a "new and original show", adding that the studio would "vigorously defend against these meritless claims".But in a 33-page opinion published on Wednesday, a three-judge panel unanimously upheld an earlier ruling that Crichton's estate had presented enough evidence to pursue its claim. Warner Bros had sought to have the lawsuit dismissed on appeal, arguing the shows shared only "generic similarities" common to "any dramatic story involving emergency room doctors".The judges said they had compared the opening episode scripts for the two shows and found sufficient similarities in plot, themes, dialogue, mood, setting, pace, characters, graphic injury detail and sequence of events. Sherri Crichton said: "I am deeply gratified by the Court of Appeal decision and look forward to discovery and to our case, which affects writers, creators, and their families and estates, being presented to a jury."Warner Bros has not yet commented on the latest ruling.

schema.headline: The Pitt and ER are similar enough for lawsuit to proceed, judge rules

title: Nvidia, SpaceX lose billions in market value as AI stocks plummet
description: Major tech firms including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla have lost hundreds of billions of dollars in market value, and more than $2 trillion was wiped fro
body: Major tech firms including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla have lost hundreds of billions of dollars in market value, and more than $2 trillion was wiped from the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite stock index in a market rout.Shares in firms across the tech and artificial intelligence sectors plummeted, partly driven by concerns of tougher regulation following Democratic wins in key data centre states.Those losses dragged the Nasdaq down by more than 5.5%, losing an estimated $2.5tn in market capitalisation, according to Dow Jones data, while other key US stock indexes also saw big losses.Following the election, some tech leaders said they needed to put more effort into marketing data centres and AI.Democrats in races across the US  campaigned to slow the onslaught of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology.Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector.Shares in companies heavily exposed to AI data centres, including crucial chipmakers and semiconductor manufacturers, fell sharply on Thursday, highlighting investor concerns that had already been growing.Nvidia shares slid more than 9%, knocking more than $400m off the firm's market value.Other chipmakers also suffered, with AMD and Micron both dropping by more than 17%. Intel shares also dropped, down 10.3%, while memory card maker SanDisk plunged more than 22%.The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which tracks the performance of 30 of the largest companies involved in semiconductor production, fell by more than 12%.Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300m off the firms' market value on Thursday.Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas was turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday night.The stock falls also hit other major US stock indexes. The S&P 500 index fell by 4.4% by the end of trading, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average erased gains made on Wednesday to close down more than 3.4%.The Nasdaq Composite fall was so large it is now in what market watchers call correction territory, which is where an index or company value falls at least 10% below its recent high.Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said the steep sell-off on the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 was sending shockwaves into other markets."Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard," she said."Fears that the vast sums poured into AI infrastructure may not deliver the returns investors have been banking on are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction."Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms.OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board."A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California on Wednesday evening.Meta's president Dina Powell McCormick said that the industry needed to put more effort into selling AI as a good idea."I think we need to double and triple down on telling the story," she told the WSJ conference.Alongside the immediate impacts of the US mid-term elections, some investors have become concerned that AI shares could be in a bubble that is due a correction.

schema.headline: Nvidia, SpaceX lose billions in market value as AI stocks plummet

title: French protests see numbers surge as unions join strikes over high cost of living
description: More than 600,000 protesters have taken part in rallies and marches across France, according to France's interior ministry, with five unions joining a
body: More than 600,000 protesters have taken part in rallies and marches across France, according to France's interior ministry, with five unions joining a day of action demanding more money for wages and public services.The left-wing CGT union put the number of people taking part in Thursday's mobilisation at 1.57 million and hailed the figure as "a level unmatched" since 2023, citing big protests in Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux and Lille.As darkness fell in Paris, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said he would convene a "social conference" with unions and employers next Monday.The wave of protests began in September over poor conditions and resources at lycées (high schools), before spreading to universities, workers and a revived "yellow-vest" movement against high prices.The unions had vowed to take the co-ordinated move against the government "to the next level", and CGT chief Sophie Binet had said their message was that "the only thing that will bring this mobilisation to a halt is responding to our demands".Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez had earlier deployed 70,000 police, vowing "an extremely firm response" to any potential outbreaks of violence.Some unrest was reported in several cities. A car was set alight near the Gallieni bridge over the Rhône river in Lyon, as hundreds of activists from the radical left-wing "black bloc" clashed with police.  Clashes were also reported in the north-western city of Rennes, where the local prefect said a "hostile group of masked individuals" had gathered in front of the main union march. Tear gas was used to clear a square in the south-western city of Bordeaux and a teenager was hurt in a stabbing involving a student at a high-school blockade in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.But the trouble was not on the scale seen during the last big day of protests, on Saturday 17 October, when more than 2,000 stores were looted and historic buildings set on fire. The provisional numbers reported on Thursday were higher than on 17 October, considered  the biggest day of rallies until now when the interior ministry said 550,000 people had turned out and the unions counted 800,000. Earlier on Thursday the leader of the CFDT union, Marylise Léon, said she would be happy if the protests matched that earlier level.The head of the CFDT complained that it was not just the minimum wage that needed to increase. "We are asking for a net increase of €100 a month," Marylise Léon explained.The government has sought to appease public anger over rising prices, bringing down the cost of fuel by releasing 10 million barrels of diesel from strategic reserves. Ministers have also promised school students to reform the unpopular Parcoursup university admissions platform and eventually replace it by 2028.The prime minister said early on Thursday evening that Monday's "social conference" with unions and employers would seek to "provide answers to questions surrounding purchasing power and wages".However, the government by its own admission has little room to manoeuvre, as it looks to make tens of billions of euros in savings, in a bid to cut the budget deficit to 5% of GDP.The education ministry said that 16% of teachers had gone on strike on Thursday, and the unions said disruption had affected more than one in four lycées, which cater for 15-18 year-olds, as well as the vast majority of universities."Now it's not only about [investing in] public services in education and higher education, it's about all of the public services in France," the vice-president of the Unef student union, Alice De Brito, told the BBC.Meanwhile, a revived gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement that staged a revolt against the high cost of living several years ago has called for further blockades and protests on Friday and Saturday too.

schema.headline: French protests see numbers surge as unions join strikes over high cost of living

title: Would you take a test to see if your life will be cut short? I did - and it changed me
description: Image source, Katie DoyImage caption, Laura Sides faced a dilemma of whether to get tested to see if she had inherited her father's conditionByEmily D
body: Image source, Katie DoyImage caption, Laura Sides faced a dilemma of whether to get tested to see if she had inherited her father's conditionByEmily DoughtyIf you could find out if you had a gene that would cut your life short, would you?This is the dilemma Laura Sides faced when she was offered a test for the rare form of early onset dementia that her dad was diagnosed with in his 40s.Laura spoke to Dr Sian Williams, host of BBC Radio 4's Life Changing podcast, about her decision to take the test and how it has shaped the rest of her life.Growing up, Laura says she always felt close to her dad as they had a "similar nature". He was a GP and "the most amazing doting father," she says. When his Alzheimer's symptoms became more severe, Laura dropped out of university to care for him."We did have a really lovely time," she says, remembering trips to a lighthouse and collecting coasters. "I'd run him baths and just play music and pour jugs of hot water over his head and he loved it."Image source, Laura SidesImage caption, Laura had just celebrated her 21st birthday when she began caring for her dadIt was at a hospital appointment with her dad when a doctor told Laura she had a 50/50 chance of developing the same type of early onset Alzheimer's known as the "London variant". "All I could think was, that's a toss of a coin," she says. "I was still so involved with what was going on with him [her dad]. I just pushed it really, really deep down."Laura's dad died in 2009, just a year after her mum had died."All of a sudden I got such an overwhelming urge to leave," she says. So she booked a solo around-the-world trip, eventually settling in Melbourne, Australia.It was there that thoughts of inheriting her dad's condition "started creeping in" and she went to see a specialist in 2013. He told her a test could determine with 99.999% certainty if she would inherit early onset dementia. If she had the gene, her expected age of decline would be 46 to 48, he said."I just thought, I'm not there yet. I don't want to do that."Life Changing'Toss of a coin’ if I’d inherit dementia gene4 November 2026As Laura entered her 30s she found herself thinking about the test more and more and decided she wanted to know. But first, she had to undergo six months of genetic counselling."There's not many realms in life where you find out your fate and it can be very difficult information to process," she says.After a six-week wait for the test results to come through, the day finally arrived. Laura says she felt "extremely nervous". She had booked a table for lunch with a friend afterwards - but went into the appointment alone. "I said, 'Let's cut straight to it.' They said, 'We're really sorry, it's not good news, and you have inherited the gene.'" She remembers "almost a white blurry noise of just sitting there"."I came out of that room and my friend burst into hysterical tears." But Laura didn't react. "We went for our lunch and it was lovely. I don't know if it'd sunk in."The reality hit later. "I was angry. I felt it was so unjust. I was just too confused at how I was meant to live now. How do you live with that knowledge?"Image source, Laura SidesImage caption, Laura has taken part in medical trials all over the worldLaura began to feel a pull back home to the UK, especially as her sister was pregnant. "It doesn't make sense... to live on the other side of the world when she's going to have a baby."However, her around-the-world travels continued as she took part in medical trials before and after her diagnosis."It felt like such a positive to be involved in something out of such a negative situation."Image source, Laura SidesImage caption, Laura (right) is a chef and owns a cafe restaurant and catering business with two friendsLaura is now 43 - three years away from the age doctors predicted she will begin to notice symptoms."I keep waiting for something to sort of hit home. I guess one day I'll start declining but that doesn't keep me up at night."She is "grateful and so lucky for the people in her life". But meeting anyone new is hard. "Do I tell them? Do I not tell them? At what point do I tell them? "And more often than not, when I have told them, it ends." However she says she has been "proven wrong". "I have been shown I can be loved despite this. It fills my heart with reassurance and joy".  Laura says she had always "naively assumed" she would be a mother."[Its] one of the very few things that I never questioned that I'd be good at and I wanted to do. That's hard... but it doesn't make sense to do it. It wouldn't be fair."Image source, Laura SidesImage caption, Laura loves swimming and is aiming to swim in as many seas as possibleFor Laura, life is now about tapping in to things that "make her happy". "It's not about huge aspirations. It's not like I want to see the Grand Canyon... I want to have time now around the people that I adore and make me feel safe. "I love nature. I love being outside. I'm obsessed with being submerged in water. It sounds so corny, but...I believe it really is actually the little things are the big things."I hope I just have a wonderful few years in this world... drinking champagne and eating oysters - two of my favourite things."If you or someone you know has been affected by dementia, you can access support from the BBC Action Line.Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues raised in this story?Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: Would you take a test to see if your life will be cut short? I did - and it changed me

title: South Africa local elections: ANC under pressure to reverse decline
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, More than 500 parties are contesting the electionsByKhanyisile NgcoboReporting fromJohannesburgSouth
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, More than 500 parties are contesting the electionsByKhanyisile NgcoboReporting fromJohannesburgSouth Africans are voting in highly contested local elections likely to see a haemorrhaging of votes for the country's biggest party, the African National Congress (ANC).This year's voting season has been marked by intense campaigns that have included politicians spinning cars, watching grannies knit and even wading through giant-sized potholes. Election officials say voting is going smoothly, despite long queues at some polling stations.Leaders are campaigning to head South Africa's nearly 300 municipalities, responsible for basic service provision such as water, electricity and refuse collection.For the ANC, the elections are a chance to prove it still has what it takes to govern. The party had a disastrous showing in the last national election, when it lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since 1994 when the racist apartheid system ended.Support for the party has been dropping significantly over the years because of anger over high levels of corruption, unemployment and crime.At its peak, in 2004, the ANC got 70% of the vote in the general election. Two decades later its share dropped to 40%.Polls and pundits have predicted a further loss in these elections but President Cyril Ramaphosa has denied that his party was in a downward spiral."What I'm seeing here is that the ANC is going higher and higher and on the 4th [of November] we will show those naysayers," he told supporters at the party's final election rally on Sunday.In townships like Alexandra, north-east of Johannesburg, the ANC has traditionally had a strong supporter base but poor governance and voter apathy are unravelling this support.The BBC visited the sprawling township a week before the elections and spoke to residents to get their views. One of them was Sanele Ntombela, who is a first-time voter excited to make his voice heard.Image source, Khanyisile Ngcobo/BBCImage caption, Sanele Ntombela (left), seen here with his friends Tshiamo Mbange (centre) and Lwandle Dladla, is excited to cast his voteWe found the 18-year-old hanging out with his friends on a street corner. Most of his friends said they had no intention of voting and had not registered to do so.They cited a lack of change and deteriorating delivery of basic services.But Ntombela was looking forward to voting for the first time and thought it might lead to change."We face many challenges in Alexandra. There's rubbish everywhere and we struggle with electricity and water and many other issues," he said.Just metres away, heaps of rubbish lay gathered beneath a streetlight pole covered in election posters from the different political parties.On the other side of the street, drain water trickles through the many potholes that have gutted that part of the road.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The ANC faces immense pressure to reverse years of declineThe BBC also spoke to Zandile Mncube, who said she wouldn't vote, even though she is registered to do so.The 33-year-old woman also cited poor service delivery and performance by local leaders for her decision."It makes no difference [whether I vote or not]. Things have gotten worse over the years," she said.Alex, as the township is known, is a stone's throw away from Sandton, Africa's richest square mile, but the differences could not be starker.Sandton is known for its skyscrapers, designer shops and well-maintained roads but in Alex, houses are sandwiched together and rubbish, either piled together or left strewn across the pavement, is everywhere. The stench of raw sewage and uncollected rubbish is heavy in the air, but residents appear used to it.The issues plaguing Alexandra are not unique. A drive around Gauteng province reveals similar patterns of neglect and disrepair, especially in the townships.South of Johannesburg, Soweto looks marginally cleaner than Alexandra, but residents also complain about service delivery.Mduduzi Makhubo, 45, has lived in Soweto his entire life and he told the BBC of the community's daily struggles with accessing water and electricity. "Every Monday we know we won't have water after 2pm," he said.Makhubo is registered to vote and intends to use his vote to deal with the "arrogance" he says local leaders have towards residents and "change the status quo".These areas offer a small, but important, glimpse into the state of South Africa's local governance.Years of reports by the auditor-general have highlighted the dire state of most of South Africa's 257 municipalities.A recent report only gave 39 clean audits - the highest ranking a public entity can achieve - between 2024 and 2025. None of Gauteng's three metro cities, Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni, featured in this list.Earlier this year auditor-general Tsakani Maluleke said Johannesburg "needs ongoing attention". "If we don't that, we are going to continue on this slide where financial health deteriorates [and] where service delivery continues to be compromised, which is what we are living," she told lawmakers.The city has been labelled "effectively bankrupt" due to the dire state of its finances. Dirty streets, unstable electricity supply and persistent water issues have been common for years.Experts the BBC spoke to agreed that all eyes will be on Africa's wealthiest city as well as the country's seven other biggest municipalities, or metros, particularly those in Gauteng when the results come in.Melanie VerwoerdThe expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever doneOf South Africa's eight metros, only three are governed by a single party. In Gauteng, all three metros are governed by coalition governments, with the ANC the largest party.But that might change.Political analyst Melanie Verwoerd said the elections would be a "verdict ... and judgment" on the ANC."And the expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done," she said.Several polls point to a continued decline in support for the party in Wednesday's election, contested by over 500 political parties.One, conducted by Ipsos, put the ANC's support at 30%, down from the 46% it got at the last local elections in 2021.The same poll, along with others, points to a slight increase in electoral support for the Democratic Alliance (DA), especially in Johannesburg. Ipsos predicts the DA will garner 25% support in this election, up from 22% last time.DA leader Helen Zille has been vying for the mayoral chain in the city and her unusual campaign has attracted a lot of attention.The former Cape Town mayor has been captured swimming in crater-sized potholes, ziplining over sinkholes and riding into her final rally in the city in a classic BMW 325i, known locally as a "Gusheshe".She believes the DA is the country's best choice for a government, telling local radio broadcaster 702 last week that "towns and cities that work best are under DA governance".Verwoerd, a former ANC MP and South Africa's ambassador to Ireland, predicted that coalitions would continue being the order of the day across Gauteng.These types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic at a local level and the constant change in leadership, usually caused by parties falling out with each other, has affected service delivery in many municipalities.Image source, Khanyisile Ngcobo/BBCImage caption, Zandile Mncube says things have got worse in her township over the yearsVerwoerd said in her view, the most stable coalitions would be those that replicate what the ANC and DA have done on a national level, where the historic rivals have agreed to share power.Reflecting on Cape Town, she said it was unlikely that the DA would lose control of the municipality. The coastal city is widely considered the country's best-performing metro and has been run by the DA since the late 2000s when it unseated the ANC.Ethekwini, which includes the port city of Durban in KwaZulu-Natal, would be a "different story", Verwoerd said.The uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party has been projected to perform well in the area but it is unclear if it will secure the outright majority needed to run the metro. Polls suggest it won't and will need partners to form a government.The party was founded by former South African President Jacob Zuma and was the biggest party across his home province of KwaZulu-Natal in the 2024 provincial election.Verwoerd reflected that while various options were on the table for the party, forming a government would be "very messy" given its refusal to work with either the ANC or DA.A confident Zuma, addressing supporters on Sunday, vowed to take control of a number of municipalities after the elections.Another political analyst Dr Levy Ndou echoed Verwoerd's assessment, saying that a coalition between the DA and ANC seemed unavoidable in most metros."We're not sure whether the arrangement of the government of national unity could have the potential to influence how the metros are going to be run," he said.Both experts also spoke about the declining voter turnout in South Africa's elections. Over 29 million citizens are registered to vote, but the turnout, especially among young people, has seen a steady decline.Ndou attributed this to the "calibre" of the candidates campaigning and the lack of visibility of local councillors, who are often the ones elected to lead their neighbourhoods, in election campaigns.South Africa's electoral commission has seven days to announce the results, but parties have 14 days to form a governing structure.

schema.headline: South Africa local elections: ANC under pressure to reverse decline

title: California Governor Gavin Newsom commutes sentences for state's 548 death row inmates
description: California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison
body: California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison. "We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter.The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed an inmate since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978.The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president.Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday. Newsom explained in his letter that he is exercising his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences to life without the possibility of parole. "After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom said. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us".California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates. Newsom had previously ordered a halt to the death penalty in the state in 2019.Newsom, describing his decision as a difficult but "righteous action", said that although many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die, he has concluded that "the state cannot morally kill them".He said that by every measure, California's system for administering the death penalty "is a failure", and that it has not and cannot be fairly applied, resulting in the conviction of innocent people.Life without the possibility of parole is the most severe punishment he can lawfully impose and that the state can ethically enforce, he said.He acknowledged that his clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians and said that it will "always weigh heavily on me"."As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," he wrote. "For this reason, I am compelled to follow my conscience and, as authorised by our Constitution, take this action for the welfare of the State of California."Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governors.The decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee in late September and while executions have been on the rise in the US. There are three executions scheduled for Thursday in Indiana, Florida and Alabama.Most of Newsom's action on Thursday will need court approval, CalMatters reported. For the commutations of the nearly 400 prisoners convicted of multiple felonies, at least four of seven judges on the California Supreme Court have to sign off.Anthony D Romero, the executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, applauded Newsom's action."These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," Romero said."By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialised injustice head-on."On the federal level, President Donald Trump, a long-time supporter of the death penalty, has described capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".In 2020, during his first term, he ended a nearly two-decade moratorium on the federal death penalty, by ordering 13 executions over a six-month period.While the moratorium returned under President Biden, on the first day of Trump's second term in 2025, he signed an executive order that re-instated the death penalty. No federal executions have been carried out since he signed it, however. In the US, both the federal government and local states authorities can order executions.The death penalty is legal in 27 states, but has been abolished in 23 states and Washington DC, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a national non-profit.California, which primarily uses lethal injection for executions, used to house male death row prisoners in San Quentin State Prison north of San Francisco, and female inmates in the Central California Women's Facility in the Central Valley. But a 2016 ballot measure allowed for their transfer to other facilities that provide a necessary level of security, according to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation.

schema.headline: California Governor Gavin Newsom commutes sentences for state's 548 death row inmates

title: Melania Trump calls for lasting Ukraine truce as she hosts Russian and Ukrainian officials
description: US First Lady Melania Trump called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine as she welcomed Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House fol
body: US First Lady Melania Trump called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine as she welcomed Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House following last week's truce in the southern region of Kherson.Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire, which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering."The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.The unusual White House event saw senior Ukrainian and Russian officials meet away from the setting of official US-brokered peace talks they have been holding without success since last year.The delegations were made up of Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova, as well as Ukrainian MP Davyd Arakhamia and Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev.Melania Trump was credited by all for playing a key though unspecified role in the ceasefire, and all parties conveyed to her the gratitude of the Russian and Ukrainian presidents.The US first lady said she had "reviewed demining plans, aerial images, assessed roadways, and discussed evacuation routes, hospital access, vehicles, and medical resources" during the truce."Last week in Oleshky and neighbouring areas of Kherson, people experienced the simple joys of life for the first time since 2022," Trump said. "They walked down familiar streets without fear of explosions."She thanked both Volodymyr Zelensky and Vladimir Putin, making no reference to the origins of the war, which began when the Russian president launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and which has caused thousands of civilian casualties and the displacement of millions. Dmitriev, a businessman and Kremlin special envoy who has previously represented Moscow during peace talks with Ukraine, thanked Trump for "saving and touching so many lives"."Let us continue making a humanitarian contribution together; this is within our power," Dmitriev said, before gifting Melania Trump a framed drawing by an 11-year-old Oleshky evacuee.He also praised Trump for her work on reuniting children separated from their families by the war. These include children allegedly abducted by Russia.Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads Zelensky's party in parliament who has also been part of the Ukrainian negotiating team, said the Oleshky ceasefire had constituted the "biggest de-escalation since 2022"."We are creating a momentum where both sides are learning the… mechanics of how to actually keep the peace when the peace comes," he added. He acknowledged that the "political track" of negotiations to end the conflict was "complex" but said Ukrainians were asking Melania Trump "to keep going and find new missions and de-escalate more."At the end of the event, Trump  handed Dmitriev and Arakhamia two letters to be hand-delivered to their respective presidents.The White House later said Melania Trump had invited her guests to view two historic artifacts which she had "personally selected as powerful symbols of peace".One was an 18th Century medicine chest which was removed from the White House when the British set it on fire in 1812. "Once adversaries, the United States and Great Britain ultimately established a strong alliance," the White House said.The second artifact was a cup gifted in 1899 to the French ambassador in recognition of his efforts to bring the Spanish-American war to an end.Melania Trump has generally remained discreet on foreign policy matters, and neither Moscow nor Kyiv have elaborated on the nature or extent of her involvement in coordinating the delicate ceasefire - the most enduring and widespread of the war so far.A source who works in the local government of the Kherson region told the BBC that work on the Oleshky evacuation had been ongoing for almost a year. However, the source said, "at a certain point other individuals became involved, seemingly after most of the groundwork had already been laid and subsequently began taking credit for the progress that had been made."It was difficult to determine exactly who had played what role and at which stage of the process, the source acknowledged, adding that "those who had been directly involved in the negotiations for nearly a year were eventually prohibited from communicating publicly about the matter."Speaking after the meeting in the White House had taken place, President Zelensky said the success of the Oleshky ceasefire "had proved a very simple thing: when Putin wants the fighting to stop, it stops.""The same applies to our people who are held in Russian captivity. When Putin wants, they go home."A source close to American officials shared a similar assessment, implying to the BBC that despite the outward praise, "the person who made [the ceasefire] possible, whether we like it or not, is essentially Putin.""And this was done in order to pass the ball to [Donald] Trump... so that it would have some positive effect for his midterm elections."There has been no change whatsoever in Russia's position, Ukrainian political analyst Dmytro Levus told the BBC. Moscow "agreed to it because there was pressure from the American side... In doing so, the Russians confirmed Zelenskyy's words that, when necessary, it turns out Russia can quickly stop firing and even maintain that ceasefire."As the frontline region of Kherson experienced its first six days of peace in several years, the rest of Ukraine continued to come under Russian attack. This week, several drone and missile attacks killed and injured civilians across the country. On Monday alone, more than 40 people were killed in a single Russian strike on an aid distribution centre in the region of Zaporizhzhia. More are thought to still be buried under the rubble.Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko in Kyiv

schema.headline: Melania Trump calls for lasting Ukraine truce as she hosts Russian and Ukrainian officials

title: Russell Brand is being investigated over two new rape complaints, police say
description: Image source, Zeynep Demir/Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, Brand has been found guilty of rape and sexual assault, following a three-week trial
body: Image source, Zeynep Demir/Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, Brand has been found guilty of rape and sexual assault, following a three-week trial at Southwark Crown Court ByHelena WilkinsonNews correspondentUpdated 6 hours agoWarning: Details of rape and sexual assaultRussell Brand is being investigated over rape allegations made by two more women, it can now be reported.The disgraced comedian has been found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault by a jury of eight men and four women at Southwark Crown Court, following a three-week trial.More victims are likely to come forward following his conviction, the detective who led the police investigation has said.Det Supt Andy Furphy, from the Metropolitan Police, said he hoped other women would gain "courage" and "confidence" from the guilty verdicts.Brand was found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.'Ruthless'Brand had initially been coy and quiet in police interviews, said Furphy, but became bolder as officers continued to question him."As he gets used to something, he becomes more emboldened by it," Furphy said. "You can certainly see that in his offending."Hundreds of people were interviewed as part of the investigation and officers said several witnesses came forward, some of whom had previously had a sexual relationship with Brand. Katy Perry, the US singer who was married to Brand from 2010 to 2012, was not interviewed.Brand, 51, who was described in court as "ruthless" and a "sexual predator", was once one of the UK's most high-profile and in-demand entertainers.Some of the women said they had been left "haunted for years" by what he did to them.Speaking to the BBC, officers working on the three-year Metropolitan Police investigation described how bringing Brand to justice was not without its challenges.Image source, Chris Jackson/Getty ImagesImage caption, Katy Perry, the US singer who was married to Brand from 2010 to 2012, was not interviewed by police as part of the investigation Allegations about Brand's behaviour first emerged in the media in September 2023.The Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches programme jointly reported that four women had accused him of rape, sexual assault and emotional abuse - claims he strongly denied.The investigation into other reports against Brand began soon after the story broke."We kind of assumed that people might want to come forward," Furphy said, "and people came forward."Victim reports were made to forces across the country and the Met set up a dedicated team of officers to lead the investigation, which it called Operation Actinolite. Officers said they have since taken more than 340 witness statements - including from Brand's former employers, his ex-colleagues and associates.One officer was assigned to read Brand's books, watch his stand-up routines and DVDs and listen to his podcasts to help build the case.Brand's high profile and the intense media scrutiny around him proved a challenge to officers, said Furphy.Another complexity for the team was the allegations were all "non-recent". The earliest dated back 27 years. It meant there was no CCTV and no forensic evidence to work with.  Furphy said police had to look for other ways to build their case."Can we look at where the victims were at the time? Who did they speak to in the aftermath of it? Did they tell anybody else? What other available material is there for us to review that might lend some weight to it? Just because it's non-recent doesn't mean that we can't solve it at all."A former friend of Brand's was called to court to give evidence for the prosecution, while a statement from the parents of one of the women was heard.The entertainer's former personal assistant, who worked closely with Brand, told the jury about his "insane sexual appetite".'Deeply uncomfortable' processTwo months after the police investigation began, Brand was interviewed under caution for the first time. He was interviewed on two further occasions in the following months.In each interview he provided officers with a prepared statement, which said he did not recognise the complainants or recall the alleged incidents and that if any sexual activity had taken place, it would have been consensual. He then answered "no comment" to the officers' questions.Charges were brought against Brand in early April 2025: one count of rape, one count of oral rape, two charges of sexual assault and one allegation of indecent assault. The final charge would later be changed to attempted indecent assault at his trial.The charges all related to women who had come forward since the initial Channel 4 documentary.The following month he appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court, in London. He was swarmed by camera crews, so much so that it took him more than two minutes to walk the short distance to the court door. At a later court hearing he pleaded not guilty to the charges.Meanwhile, women continued to come forward with more allegations.In July 2025, Brand was interviewed for a fourth time before being charged with further offences: one count of rape and one count of sexual assault. He also denied those allegations.And then on 14 October 2026, accompanied by his wife Laura, the actor and comedian entered the glass dock at London's Southwark Crown Court for the start of his trial.Image source, Leon Neal/Getty ImagesImage caption,  Brand arrives at court ahead of his trial, accompanied by his wife Laura  The women each came to court and gave evidence to the jury from behind a screen, with Brand listening from the dock. At times they cried as they gave their evidence.Furphy believes there may be more women who will now come forward."I think it's likely - potentially - that other women will come forward," he said. "They'll probably gain some courage and some confidence from what's happened in the courtroom over the last few weeks."He credits the women for their bravery during what has been at times a "deeply uncomfortable" process. "They are courageous, determined women and our focus has always been on them, not Russell Brand."Russell Brand on TrialYou can follow analysis and further insights on the BBC podcast Russell Brand on Trial - available on BBC Sounds, YouTube, iPlayer, or wherever you get your BBC podcasts

schema.headline: Russell Brand is being investigated over two new rape complaints, police say

title: US-funded vaccine trial on babies cancelled in Guinea-Bissau after uproar
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Like many neighbouring countries, Guinea-Bissau waits until babies are six weeks old to vaccinate them agains
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Like many neighbouring countries, Guinea-Bissau waits until babies are six weeks old to vaccinate them against hepatitis B, while the WHO says it should be done at birth (file photo)ByBasma El Atti and Makuochi OkaforBBC AfricaA proposed trial of a hepatitis B vaccine on newborn babies in Guinea-Bissau has been cancelled following accusations that the trial was "unethical" and "neocolonial".The trial was funded by the US, under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has a long record of expressing scepticism about vaccines. Police have seized a batch of vaccines from the research centre at the heart of the controversy. The proposed trial drew international criticism because it planned to withhold a vaccine recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) from half of the participating newborns.Some public health experts argued that the proposed trial raised broader questions about whether vulnerable populations in African countries were being asked to take risks that researchers would not accept in wealthier countries.The BBC has asked the US department of health and human services for comment.Here is what you need to know.What was the trial?The study was planned at the Bandim Health Project, a research centre that has operated in Guinea-Bissau since 1978. It was designed to involve 14,000 newborns, with half receiving a hepatitis B vaccine shortly after birth and the other half not being given the shot.Bandim said the trial aimed to investigate whether the hepatitis B vaccine given at birth has broader health effects beyond preventing infection. Previous studies in The Gambia and Guinea-Bissau have raised questions about a possible link to increased mortality.Researchers argued that because Guinea-Bissau does not currently offer routine hepatitis B vaccinations at birth, despite WHO recommendations, they have a unique opportunity to study its effects before such vaccines are introduced in 2028. But critics questioned the ethics of withholding the vaccine from some babies, particularly in one of the world's poorest countries, where the infection is widespread.The Trump administration funded the proposed study, with the CDC awarding the University of Southern Denmark (SDU) $1.6m (£1.2m) in December 2025.What did the WHO say?Walter Kazadi Mulombo, the WHO representative in Guinea-Bissau, told the BBC they became concerned after receiving questions about the study and finding no publicly available protocol.He said the main ethical concern was that the trial would withhold an intervention already proven to protect newborns against hepatitis B."The vaccine has been used for more than 30 years in more than 115 countries," he said. "A study that will withhold that intervention from other newborns is unethical."He warned that babies could be exposed to the virus during childbirth if their mothers were infected, as well as later in life.Nearly a fifth of the population of Guinea-Bissau are infected with hepatitis B, a viral infection that affects the liver.Those infected during infancy are particularly likely to develop chronic infections, which kill up to 25% of people, mostly through liver failure or liver cancer, according to data published in 2020.The WHO is working with the government to bring forward the birth-dose vaccine. "The country had been expected to add it to its routine immunisation schedule in 2028, but officials are considering introducing it in the first quarter of next year," Mulombo said.Guinea-Bissau currently vaccinates children against hepatitis B at six weeks, which means it is less effective.Why did Guinea-Bissau reject the trial?Guinea-Bissau's government prohibited hepatitis B vaccine trials involving children in January. At the time, it requested a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study.Health Minister Quinhin Nantote said in October that the suspension remained in force and had not been overturned by the Council of Ministers after reports emerged claiming that the trial would be taking place after all."We were surprised to learn from media reports that the study might proceed," Nantote said. "We are outraged because even I, as the minister responsible for this sector, was not informed."The dispute intensified after the SDU said a revised study protocol had received ethical approval "from the relevant authorities in Guinea-Bissau", which Nantote denied. Dr Gavin Yamey, a professor of global health and public policy at Duke University in the US, criticised the proposal."The proposed trial reeks of neocolonialism," he told the BBC, questioning why the research was not being conducted in Denmark.His criticism centred on the decision to withhold a recommended vaccine from some newborns in a country where hepatitis B is widespread.SDU dean Jakob Grauslund said the trial had never started, no babies had been enrolled and no vaccinations administered as part of the research.Was the trial approved by anyone?The SDU said it had received a separate, positive assessment from the university's own research ethics committee.Grauslund said the university had sought an additional independent assessment, although Danish law did not require one.He added that the relevant Danish statutory research ethics bodies were unable to undertake the review. Following the approval from the SDU's ethics committee, Grauslund decided that the project could proceed.He, however, stressed that this did not replace the separate authorisation required from Guinea-Bissau's authorities.What has happened to the vaccines?On 19 October, Guinea-Bissau's Judicial Police searched the Bandim Health Project's facilities in the capital, Bissau, and seized a batch of hepatitis B vaccines.Police said the batch was intended for vaccinating children but did not disclose how many doses had been seized or the specific grounds for the investigation.They stressed that the seizure did not, in itself, mean the vaccines were defective or unsafe.The police have not explicitly said whether their investigation relates to the proposed trial, the importation of the vaccines or other circumstances surrounding the batch.Grauslund said he could not comment on the seizure of the vaccines.Who is funding the research?The proposed trial was funded by the US government at a time of significant changes to vaccine policy under President Donald Trump and Health Secretary Kennedy. Under Kennedy's leadership, a US vaccine panel attempted to end a longstanding recommendation that all newborns receive a hepatitis B vaccine at birth, but a federal judge later blocked this, along with other changes to vaccine policy made by the Trump administration.Critics have questioned whether the research could help support that policy shift, although the study's stated aim was to investigate potential effects of the vaccine beyond preventing infection.Kennedy has praised the Danish researchers as "the deities of vaccine research", and cited earlier findings from their work in support of concerns about vaccine safety. A subsequent study by some of the same researchers, however, found no evidence of the previously reported effect.There is no evidence that the proposed trial was designed to justify a change in US policy.You may also be interested in:

schema.headline: US-funded vaccine trial on babies cancelled in Guinea-Bissau after uproar

title: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
description: Figure caption, With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?ByWashington correspondentUpdated 03:47 GMTVice-President JD Vance sent shockwav
body: Figure caption, With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?ByWashington correspondentUpdated 03:47 GMTVice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election."The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington.  While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.Figure caption, Could Democrats in Congress end the war in Iran?Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake."If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.It was a striking statement, and one with no recent precedent: it's hard to recall a similar moment in recent US political history when a sitting vice-president has so sharply broken with the president on a signature foreign policy issue.Then came an arguably even greater surprise: Trump - who typically demands steadfast loyalty from his senior advisers - agreed with Vance that the midterms were "largely" decided by the war. He added that he would "do it again" if given the same choices.Image source, ReutersDrawing contrasts with Trump will be a delicate balancing act if Vance seeks the presidency, Byman added.That balance was on display in Vance's post. The vice president didn't mention Trump by name and attributed much of his election results analysis to unnamed pollsters.Vance "put his toe in the water to see what he's going to do," Ashley Davis, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.Beyond the Iran war criticism, Vance also offered a political roadmap that could preview a possible presidential campaign. He distilled the party's strategy to win back voters into a neat four-point gameplan:  "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."The list encapsulated much of Vance's worldview since bursting onto the national political scene, and read like the core argument in a future stump speech.The BBC has contacted Vance's office for comment.Of course, the next presidential election is still two years away. Vance is expected to run but hasn't made an official decision, and aides insist that he's still mulling it over.It's also up for debate exactly how much Vance broke from Trump. Vance showed the message to Trump before posting it online, according to The New York Times.Trump, for his part, could change his mind and make clear he'll brook no dissent from Vance or anyone else.The president has been circumspect about who he'd support to succeed him as the 2028 Republican presidential nominee. Trump has praised Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on several occasions, but hasn't said when - or if – he'd make an endorsement.The president appears to relish the guessing game of who he'd back to carry on his political movement, even in the past floating the idea that he'd continue to a third term (which is barred by the US Constitution).Vance's midterms missive might not be that significant in the end. Or it could have been the starting gun for the 2028 race and the battle for the post-Trump Republican Party.Nardine Saad contributed reporting.

schema.headline: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war

title: Hoax bomb threats target European airlines and airports for second time in a week
description: Noble said they remained on board for two-and-a-half hours while police and military personnel carried out checks, including searches with sniffer dog
body: Noble said they remained on board for two-and-a-half hours while police and military personnel carried out checks, including searches with sniffer dogs.The passengers were later told they would be taken to an airport in Paris and another plane would fly them on to Rome.Philip Baum, professor of aviation security at the University of Coventry, said the industry "faces multiple bomb threats every single day" but he had been "surprised" by this week's incidents.A flight is diverted "only when the threat is credible and the authorities believe there is a potential of explosive device on board", he said.He said the concern was that "if you issue enough hoax threats, then complacency could set in and a real threat could be ignored - or they could be a diversion".Marco Chan, an aviation expert at Kingston University, told the BBC the threats were "most likely a hoax, but the system is right to treat it as real".He said they were being viewed by some experts as "possibly part of a pattern of cheap, deniable disruption" to air travel.Hoaxes can also come from copycats, he said, but "three days of incidents is too small a sample to separate coordination from contagion".Two days ago, seven European flights, including two from the UK, were searched after bomb threats were made. No explosives were found on any of the planes after searches.On Monday, a Wizz Air flight travelling from London Luton Airport to Sofia was escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet to Budapest after a mid-air bomb threat.

schema.headline: Hoax bomb threats target European airlines and airports for second time in a week

title: Cristiano Ronaldo retirement: Why has Portugal legend retired from international game?
description: Cristiano Ronaldo's old rival Leo Messi left Argentina less than a month ago with a nation applauding him.The Portugal legend has gone another way, an
body: Cristiano Ronaldo's old rival Leo Messi left Argentina less than a month ago with a nation applauding him.The Portugal legend has gone another way, and it was always going to be the case.The 41-year-old announced his international retirement after 23 years but also after a fallout with coach Jorge Jesus which was resolved with a sanction of 30 days, that had already been served, and a fine of 255 euros.It was the punishment imposed on the Portuguese striker for leaving the team's training camp without permission. Jesus kept him on the bench for one match and said he did not plan to start him in the next, so Ronaldo went home.His last appearance came on 24 September against Wales. He ends his international career with 146 goals in 234 games.A message went around Portugal with a big thank you for everything, calling Ronaldo a global ambassador and an inspiration to millions. Even so, the way it ended leaves a bit of a bitter taste.Was he going to be named in the next squad? Possibly, as Jesus said the door was open and the decision was Ronaldo's. What is clear is that he was no longer an automatic starter, and Cristiano has never handled that well.So is this another hissy fit? Partly, yes. He reacted the way he always has when a coach questions his place. But the label hides how much he adapted over the years.Such a pattern appears with almost every man who sat on the Portuguese bench - there were clashes, but also communion with managers and team-mates that help explain this ending.When a young Ronaldo first joined the squad, he arrived at camp with his baseball cap on backwards, enormous sunglasses and headphones turned up so loud they could be heard from a distance.He would not take the cap off to eat among veterans like Luis Figo and Rui Costa. Luiz Felipe Scolari saw an extraordinary player who was immature and obsessed with showing off. He reprimanded him in public, then told him privately that if he changed his attitude, he would one day captain Portugal.The first great disappointment came early, and it came at home. At 19, Ronaldo played in the final of Euro 2004 at the Estadio da Luz in Lisbon, in front of a country that had convinced itself the trophy was already on its way.A single headed goal by Angelos Charisteas was enough for unfancied Greece to win it by surprise. When the final whistle went, Ronaldo could not hold back the tears, and the image of the teenager crying on his own pitch travelled everywhere.It was a painful way to learn what a final costs, and it left him with a hunger that never really went away.Figo owned the number 7 at the time, so Ronaldo had to have 17. Figo helped him settle but had no intention of making it easy. When he left the national team in 2006, the shirt and the team became Ronaldo's.In September 2005, before a qualifier in Russia, Scolari and Figo went to his room to tell him his father had died. Scolari offered to send him home. Ronaldo chose to play, asked his team-mates to behave as normal, and spent time in the dressing room doing ball tricks.That was his way to cope with the expected but still hugely hurtful passing of his alcoholic dad.  He later called Scolari "father". That way the national team had become the place that held him together.Things went sour with Carlos Queiroz. After the 2010 World Cup exit against Spain, asked to explain a poor performance, Ronaldo told journalists to ask the coach. His influence in the camp had grown so large it changed routines and habits, which explains why the coach felt undermined.The sociologist Joao Nuno Coelho offers the best lens on how Portugal sees him. In his analysis, the national team became a representation of Portuguese identity and of the country's need to be seen internationally.In years of economic hardship and a crisis of confidence, a team that won admiration abroad was important beyond football.Ronaldo stood at the centre of that need and created contradictory feelings. Some Portuguese questioned his individualism and his ego, and not everyone saw themselves in his personality.Coelho explains criticising him became more difficult as time went by. The country wanted to be proud of him and sometimes felt uneasy at the same time.The former international Jorge Andrade told me some supporters preferred figures like Figo, Eusebio, Paulo Futre or Rui Costa. Even so, Portugal was proud to have him. And with the titles, the doubts eased.Under Fernando Santos in 2016, he changed. He accepted playing as a centre forward next to Nani - he had never taken a coach's instructions so naturally.After the opening draw with Iceland, he told Nani in private that he trusted Santos, and the dressing room began to see a real captain. After missing a penalty against Austria, he barely slept. Santos woke up and found him already awake.At the training camp in Marcoussis, he took a fan's megaphone and told supporters Portugal had won nothing yet. He was enjoying the leadership role.In the final in Paris, he left the pitch in tears, injured. He had not had the best tournament, with a muscle complaint that did not let him perform at his best.Nani took the armband. At half-time Ronaldo pulled himself together to encourage his team-mates, and before extra time, still limping, he told Eder he would score.And Eder did.But the old instinct never fully disappeared. During extra-time, Ronaldo stood in the technical area giving orders until the fourth official sent him back. Other coaches I consulted found it excessive.His greatest strength, the need to influence every result, also made limits hard to accept.When he debuted in 2003, Portugal was still searching for its first major title. Some players mark an era, and others change a national team for good. He belongs to the second group.That night in July 2016 gave Portugal its first European Championship.Three years later he scored a hat-trick against Switzerland to put them into the first Nations League final, which Portugal won. In 2025 he lifted a second Nations League at an age when most players have retired.No one has scored more goals for a national side, and no one has pulled on the Portugal shirt more times.Under his influence, Portugal stopped being a gifted team and became one that arrives at every tournament expecting to contend, while a whole generation of players came through a dressing room where he decided what the standard was.Coelho's point holds here as well: a small country found a way to be noticed, and for two decades he was its face.After 2016 the question around him changed. Fewer asked whether he was selfish, and more asked whether Portugal depended on him too much.In the World Cup in 2018, he scored three against Spain, including a free-kick after 45 attempts in major tournaments, and the team still went out to Uruguay.After a difficult 2026 World Cup, much was made of him still starting up front when in fact statistically that was his best period.Under Roberto Martinez, with 28 goals in 37 games, 0.756 per match, improves the 0.624 with Santos.The federation has announced a special tribute to honour his contribution, and that is necessary as the exit has not left fans room for a celebration they want to be part of.Not only they grew up with him, he took them to places they had not yet been.

schema.headline: Cristiano Ronaldo retirement: Why has Portugal legend retired from international game?

title: 'All this food is now useless': Piles of rubbish after shop freezers hit by cyber-attack
description: In dozens of supermarkets across several European countries, a huge amount of food has been dumped after refrigerators and freezers were targeted in a
body: In dozens of supermarkets across several European countries, a huge amount of food has been dumped after refrigerators and freezers were targeted in a cyber-attack.Belgium and Luxembourg saw some of the worst damage, with 40 Delhaize supermarkets affected, and incidents also took place in stores across Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland. In a branch of supermarket Delhaize in Hoeilaart, just outside the Belgian capital Brussels, the BBC's Europe correspondent Nick Beake found frozen pizzas and ice cream among a mountain of food having to be scrapped. This branch estimated the cost of the damage running to more than €100,000 (£83,500).

schema.headline: 'All this food is now useless': Piles of rubbish after shop freezers hit by cyber-attack

title: How rapist Russell Brand was never far from controversy
description: Russell Brand has been found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.The comedian and actor, 51, has been remanded in custody a
body: Russell Brand has been found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.The comedian and actor, 51, has been remanded in custody and will be sentenced on Monday.The charges dated from 1999 to 2009 and concerned six women. They are all entitled to lifelong anonymityBBC correspondent Sima Kotecha explains how the trial unfolded.Follow this story live.

schema.headline: How rapist Russell Brand was never far from controversy
